body: @Riteo Do you think Wayland can support this feature?
@scgm0 yea, I don't see why it should not.

> @scgm0 yea, I don't see why it should not.

It seems that the logic of Wayland is much more complex. I can't simply use an `if` statement to make the main window hide as I could in X11. The key seems to lie in `libdecor_frame_unref(ws.libdecor_frame)`? Without using it, the main window turns into a black window after calling hide, but with it, the main window can't be made to reappear. I don't know much about these window protocols—they're too complicated.

> @scgm0 yeah the Wayland backend has a few extra abstractions for various reasons. We basically have a custom "driver" (like `gl_manager` and the vulkan rendering context device driver) but for Wayland stuff that runs in its own thread and has a separate, simpler state.
> 
> I think the call you're looking for is `WaylandThread::window_destroy`, which should work fine paired with the graphic driver calls.
> 
> I have currently limited programming capacity due to what I assume is a burn-out, but if you want I can take a shot at this as soon as I find the chance.

Yes, I found `WaylandThread::window_destroy`, and inside it I discovered `libdecor_frame_unref(ws.libdecor_frame);`.
![图片](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/23468b3a-1d4c-48d7-b1c7-8a97db21aa15)

What I mean, is that you should be able to call `window_destroy` without issues to unmap the main window, as its state is completely different (for various reasons) from `DisplayServer`. There's no need to call `libdecor_frame_unref` manually, also because libdecor might not be available and there's a fallback code path for "native" undecorated surfaces in there.

Edit: clarifications
To be clear, if you want I can try it myself and send you a patch if I manage to let it work. Just note that I might be a bit slow because of personal reasons.

Eventually, I got stuck on the call to `libdecor_frame_unref`.

I'm sorry for the late reply. I've been dealing with some real-life issues recently, so I haven't had time to handle this PR for now.

@deralmas Could you take a look at my current code? Wayland is really complicated...

@leogott It's ready for testing now.

After an afternoon of repeated modifications and testing, the Wayland main window using Vulkan can now be properly hidden and redisplayed. However, its process is completely different from that of the Wayland main window using OpenGL, and each can only function correctly with its respective procedure (Vulkan uses `wayland_thread.window_destroy` and `show_window`, while OpenGL uses `wayland_thread.window_set_visible`). It remains uncertain whether other issues may arise.

@scgm0 I haven't given an in depth look, but from a quick glance I *think* the Vulkan method is more correct™. The renderer attaches/commits stuff all the time on its own, so telling it to stop doing that is obviously better. I think the reason you're seeing this only with Vulkan is that some compositors (such as KDE) now implement FIFO. When we detect it, we completely disable our custom throttling. This isn't yet the case with OpenGL, so it's easy to just mark the window as never ready by forcing the `ready` flag to false.

That said, I recall having weird issues with Vulkan where the engine expects a "screen" to be there for each window, at least during engine initialization. This touches the pretty advanced vulkan driver, so I can't really tell you off the top of my head if it's going to give problems, sorry xD

> I _think_ the Vulkan method is more correct™.

I tried to make GL also use VK's method, but when re-displaying the main window, `window_set_vsync_mode` in `show_window` throws an error. I'm not sure whether I should modify those existing methods, as my understanding of them is not deep enough. So, in the end, GL chose the current method.

> but when re-displaying the main window, window_set_vsync_mode in show_window throws an error

Well yea, the window does not exist as far as the WaylandThread is concerned :P

I assume that the "proper" solution would be to not call it from the DS if the window is hidden. Anyways, I don't think that the "OpenGL solution" is solid, as it assumes manual frame throttling, which is a hack in the first place.

> Well yea, the window does not exist as far as the WaylandThread is concerned :P I quickly tested it, and the error is not that the window doesn't exist, but that the V-Sync mode of the egl_manager cannot be set. ``` WARNING: Could not set V-Sync mode. at: set_use_vsync (drivers/egl/egl_manager.cpp:403) GDScript backtrace (most recent call first): [0] _on_button_pressed (res://main.gd:7) WARNING: Could not set V-Sync mode. at: set_use_vsync (drivers/egl/egl_manager.cpp:403) GDScript backtrace (most recent call first): [0] _on_button_pressed (res://main.gd:7) ```

Hmm, after commenting out `window_set_vsync_mode(wd.vsync_mode, p_window_id);`, the situation seems even more complicated. The taskbar icon reappears, but the window cannot be brought to the foreground. This issue also occurs when VK uses `wayland_thread.window_set_visible`. It's really quite complex...

> I quickly tested it, and the error is not that the window doesn't exist [snip]

Oh, right.

> Hmm, after commenting out window_set_vsync_mode(wd.vsync_mode, p_window_id);, the situation seems even more complicated.

What if you gate the egl setting by checking for `wd.visible`? I wonder if commenting the whole thing is breaking it because it doesn't initialize frame throttling for that window and gets confused. Not sure tbh.
